results.document: Medicare & You 2027
results.reference: A 7-month Initial Enrollment Period: 3 months before the month you turn 65, the birthday month, and 3 months after. PDF p.17.

results.answer:
Your first chance to sign up is the **7-month** Initial Enrollment Period. Generally, you can first sign up for Part A and/or Part B during the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.

There's an exception if your birthday falls on the 1st: your 7-month period starts 4 months before the month you turn 65, includes your birthday month, and ends 2 months after the month you turn 65. For example, if you turn 65 on June 2, your 7-month period would begin in March and end in September. If you turn 65 on June 1, your 7-month period would begin in February and end in August.

When you sign up affects when coverage starts:
- If you sign up for Part A and/or Part B during the first 3 months of your Initial Enrollment Period, in most cases, your coverage begins the first day of your birthday month.
- If you sign up the month you turn 65 or during the last 3 months of your Initial Enrollment Period, your coverage starts the first day of the month after you sign up.

If you miss this window, your enrollment may be delayed and you may have to pay a late enrollment penalty that's added to your monthly premium for as long as you have Part B.

results.answer:
For skilled nursing facility care, you generally need a hospital stay of **3 days in a row or more**. Medicare covers this care when you have a qualifying inpatient hospital stay. This means you had a prior medically necessary inpatient hospital stay of 3 days in a row or more, starting with the day the hospital admits you as an inpatient, but not including the day you leave the hospital.

Other conditions and limits:
- Your doctor must certify that you need daily skilled care (like intravenous fluids/medications or therapy) which, as a practical matter, you can only get as a skilled nursing facility inpatient.
- Medicare doesn't cover non-medical, long-term care, so a regular nursing home stay for custodial care isn't covered.

Exceptions to the 3-day rule:
- You may not need a 3-day minimum inpatient hospital stay if your doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) that's approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver.
- Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive the 3-day minimum hospital stay.

Costs per benefit period (2026 figures):
- Days 1–20: You pay $0 each day after you pay the $1,736 amount. However, you don't have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period.
- Days 21–100: You pay $217 each day.
- Days 101 and beyond: You pay all costs.

results.answer:
You can replace a lost Medicare card in a few ways:

Doctors who don't accept assignment can charge up to **15%** above the Medicare-approved amount. In many cases, the charge can't be more than 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for non-participating healthcare providers. This amount is called "the limiting charge."

The FEHB Blue Cross Blue Shield brochure puts it the same way: a physician who does not accept Medicare assignment may not bill you for more than 115% of the amount Medicare bases its payment on, called the "limiting charge." If your physician tries to collect more than allowed by law, ask the physician to reduce the charges. If the physician does not, report the physician to the Medicare carrier that sent you the MSN form.

Also, you might have to pay the entire charge at the time of service.

results.question: How do I appeal a decision about a claim under Original Medicare?
results.document: Medicare & You 2027
results.reference: Take the Medicare Summary Notice showing the item, circle it, explain why you disagree, and send it to the Medicare Administrative Contractor listed on it (or use Form CMS-20027) by the date on the MSN. PDF p.103.

results.answer:
Under Original Medicare, the appeal process works like this:

- Get the "Medicare Summary Notice" (MSN) that shows the item or service you're appealing.
- Circle the item(s) on the MSN you disagree with. Write an explanation of why you disagree with the decision. You can write on the MSN or on a separate piece of paper and attach it to the MSN.
- Include your name, phone number, and Medicare Number on the MSN. Keep a copy for your records.
- Send the MSN, or a copy, to the company that handles bills for Medicare (Medicare Administrative Contractor) listed on the MSN. You can include any information you have about your appeal, like information from your health care provider.

Instead of the MSN, you can use Form CMS-20027. To get this form, visit Medicare.gov/basics/forms-publications-mailings/forms/appeals, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to have a copy mailed to you. TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

The deadline is in the MSN. You must file your appeal by the date in the MSN. If you miss it, you may still file an appeal and get a decision if you can show good cause for missing the deadline (for example, if you have a disability, illness, or accident that delayed you from sending it by the deadline).

You'll generally get a decision from the Medicare Administrative Contractor within 60 days after they get your request. If Medicare will cover the item(s) or service(s), it will be listed on your next MSN.

Two practical tips: you can ask your doctor, supplier, or other health care provider for any information to make your appeal stronger. Keep a copy of everything related to your appeal, including copies you send to Medicare or your plan. You can also get help filing an appeal from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

OPM has determined that this plan's drug coverage is considered Creditable Coverage. This means you do not need to enroll in Medicare Part D and pay extra for prescription drug coverage. If you decide to enroll in Medicare Part D later, you will not have to pay a penalty for late enrollment as long as you keep your FEHB coverage.

**When a penalty could apply:**
- If you lose or drop your FEHB coverage and go 63 days or longer without prescription drug coverage that is at least as good as Medicare's prescription drug coverage, your monthly Medicare Part D premium will go up at least 1 percent per month for every month that you did not have that coverage.
- You will have to pay this higher premium as long as you have Medicare prescription drug coverage.
- In addition, you may have to wait until the next Annual Coordinated Election Period (October 15 through December 7) to enroll in Medicare Part D.

**If you choose to enroll in Part D anyway:** you can keep your FEHB coverage and your FEHB plan will coordinate benefits with Medicare. Medicare will pay first if you're a retired federal employee.

**Caution:** If you are an annuitant and you cancel your FEHB coverage, you may not re-enroll in the FEHB Program.

results.answer:
Generally, no. Under Basic Option you must use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits. There are no benefits for care performed by Participating and Non-participating providers.

There are exceptions:
- **Certain circumstances:** Benefits are available except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care. See Section 3 for exceptions under What you must do to get covered care.
- **Overseas care:** The Basic Option requirement to use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits does not apply when you receive overseas care.

results.question: How much is the hospital deductible I pay under Original Medicare each time I start a new benefit period?
results.document: Medicare & You 2027
results.reference: $1,736 in 2026 for each benefit period. PDF p.30 (also p.31 for skilled nursing facility care).

results.answer:
Under Original Medicare, the Part A hospital deductible is **$1,736** (2026 figure). Each time you start a new benefit period, you must pay $1,736 (in 2026) before Medicare starts to pay. After that deductible, for Days 1–60 you pay $0 each day.

You can owe it more than once a year. You must pay the Part A deductible each time you start a new benefit period. This could be multiple times in a calendar year (January–December). Your benefit period ends once you've been out of the hospital for 60 days in a row. If you're admitted to the hospital again after those 60 days, a new benefit period will start.

If you go to a skilled nursing facility after a hospital stay, you don't have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period.
